setting: Cevre bilimi dersinde gurultu kirliligi uzerine ders anlatimi
context_line: You will hear part of a lecture about noise pollution, how it is measured and how it can be reduced.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Good morning. Last week, air quality; this week, the other invisible pollutant — noise. Let me begin by being precise about the word itself.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Sound is physical: a pressure wave you can measure. Noise is a judgement — it is sound that somebody does not want. That matters, because two people in the same street, exposed to exactly the same measured level, will not report the same amount of annoyance. The gap between them is not a measurement error; it is the subject of the research.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: The unit is the decibel, and the scale is logarithmic. A rise of ten decibels represents ten times the sound energy, and is heard as roughly twice as loud. So if you double the traffic on a road, you do not add ten decibels. You add three. That is twice the energy, and here the textbook and the street part company: three decibels is the smallest change a listener can pick out in the quiet of a laboratory, but in our own roadside surveys nobody reliably reports a change until it reaches six, which is to say you have to quadruple the traffic before anybody living on it notices at all.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Measurement. A sound level meter applies a weighting, because the ear is far less sensitive to low frequencies, and the weighting used for environmental work discounts the low end heavily. The level is then averaged over time, and for policy we use a whole-day indicator which adds a penalty of five decibels to the evening and ten to the night: ask residents what actually wakes them and they do not name the motorway, nor even the night lorry, they name the delivery van reversing into the shop yard at two in the morning.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Mapping. In many countries any built-up area above a threshold population must produce a strategic noise map and refresh it every five years — not every three, the interval the older textbooks still print, which was relaxed once authorities saw what the modelling cost. The maps are modelled rather than measured. You feed in traffic counts, speeds, the heights of the buildings and the hardness of the ground, and the model predicts a level at a grid of points across each frontage. Then you count the people living behind those frontages.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: So what dominates? Road traffic, overwhelmingly. You will sometimes see it put at two thirds of the exposed population; the more recent figures put it nearer four fifths. After that the ranking is not the one you would expect. The textbook order puts railways second and aircraft third, but on the latest continent-wide count aircraft reach more people than the railways do, because flight paths run over dense suburbs while the busiest lines run through open country — and aircraft generate a far higher volume of complaint per person exposed as well.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Break road noise down. Below about forty kilometres an hour, what you are hearing is the engine and the exhaust. Above that, the dominant source is the contact between the tyre and the road surface. Which is why electric vehicles make much less difference to street noise than people expect: they are quiet in a car park and no quieter at all on a bypass.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Control, then. The hierarchy always runs in this order: at the source, along the path, at the receiver.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: At the source you can change the surface. A porous asphalt with an open texture absorbs part of the sound generated in the tyre tread. You will see five decibels quoted; on a road that has silted up after a few years, three to four is a more honest figure, and the benefit decays steadily as the pores fill. You can also change the speed: dropping a limit from fifty to thirty kilometres an hour is worth somewhere around two to three decibels, and costs almost nothing.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Along the path, the tool is the barrier, and a barrier works by breaking the line of sight between the source and the ear. If you can see the wheels, the wall isn't working. A well-placed barrier will give you five to ten decibels, and an earth bund does the same work while looking like landscape.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: And here is a myth you should be able to correct. Trees are not an acoustic barrier: a thin screen along a road does essentially nothing to the measured level. The figure people carry in their heads is something like ten metres of planting; the research suggests you need a dense belt of something closer to thirty metres before you get even a couple of decibels. What trees achieve is different: they hide the road, and people who cannot see the traffic report less annoyance at the same measured level.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: At the receiver you are into glazing, and there is a trap. Secondary glazing works, and every catalogue sells you on the thickness of the glass, but it is the width of the gap between the panes that does the work — under a hundred millimetres of gap you are buying very little; but a sealed bedroom in July is unbearable, so the window gets opened and everything that was paid for is lost. The better answer is planning: put the bedrooms on the quiet side of the building.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Two further findings. Character matters as much as level: a steady hum is tolerated far better than the same energy delivered as a series of bangs, and a tone standing out from the background provokes complaints well below the level you would predict. And control matters: noise that people believe to be necessary is reported as very much less annoying than identical noise from a source they feel they have no say over.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: The ecology, briefly — that is where the field is moving. Birds in noisy places sing at a higher pitch than the same species in quiet places, and — this is where the popular account goes wrong, it is not that they sing louder — they start earlier in the morning; the low frequencies of traffic mask the low end of their song. Some species simply thin out within a few hundred metres of a busy road, on otherwise good habitat — so a road takes away more habitat than the strip of asphalt it occupies.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: For the practical next week: you will each sign out a meter, choose two locations and log for an hour at each, in fifteen-minute blocks. One on a main road, one somewhere you would call quiet. Write down what you can hear as well as what the instrument says — that column is what we will spend the seminar arguing about.

notes: turn_index degerleri 0 tabanlidir. Bes celdirici duzeltme var: trafigin iki katina cikmasi (on desibel -> uc desibel), gurultu haritasi yenileme araligi (uc yil -> bes yil), karayolu payi (ucte iki -> yaklasik beste dort), gozenekli asfaltin kazanci (bes desibel -> uc-dort desibel), agac seridi derinligi (on metre -> otuz metre). Ingiliz Ingilizcesinde 'meter' olcum aleti, 'metre' uzunluk birimidir; ikisi de bilerek kullanildi. Metinde rakam yok. 2026-08-18 sizinti turu (L4-S4): tur 2, 3 ve 4'te yerinde ifade degisikligi yapildi, tur sayisi ve tur ici cumle sayisi degismedi. (a) tur 2: 'uc desibel en kucuk fark edilir degisim' iddiasi laboratuvara baglandi, sokak anketinde esik ALTI desibel (trafigi dorte katlamak); test 32 artik bu yerel degeri soruyor. (b) tur 3: gece cezasini ornekleyen arac 'lorry' yerine 'delivery van', motorway ve night lorry sesli rakip olarak reddediliyor; test 33 bunu soruyor. (c) tur 4: eski ders kitabi araligi acikca isaretlendi; test 34 artik guncel bes yil yerine eski UC yil degerini soruyor, bes yil celdirici oldu.
